title: The rebbe
hookLine: a Hasidic leader seen as guide and channel for his followers

lines: A LONG TABLE ON A FRIDAY NIGHT.
A CRUMB PASSED INTO THE CROWD.
cards: A long table on a Friday night. At the head sits one man, and around him, packed shoulder to shoulder, some standing on benches, are his followers. He hardly speaks.

He tastes a little of the food in front of him, and what's left is passed out into the crowd, and people reach for a crumb of it. Then someone starts a melody with no words, and the whole room picks it up.
Hasidim call a gathering like this a tish, a table. The man at the head of it has a title of his own.

teach.b: Rebbe. It's the Yiddish way of saying rabbi, and among Hasidim it means something particular: the leader of a Hasidic community, the one his followers turn to. First, the guide.

Long before Hasidism, the Mishnah gives a piece of advice in Pirkei Avot: make for yourself a teacher. Not find one, make one, as if choosing a guide is something you do on purpose. Hasidim took that seriously.
A follower brings the rebbe questions about prayer, but also about a marriage, a business, a sick child.

Hasidic teaching speaks of the tzaddik, the righteous one, and sees the rebbe this way: someone so attached to God that blessing flows through him to the people around him, and their prayers rise with his.
That's why a crumb from his plate matters to them.
Third, the bond goes both ways. A rebbe carries his followers in his heart and in his prayers, and the followers' devotion is part of how the community holds together.

teach.h: NOT EVERY JEW SEES IT THIS WAY.
teach.b: Fourth, and fairly: not every Jew sees it this way. Some Jewish communities, from early on, were wary of giving one person that much weight, and preferred to center life on study and the rabbi as a scholar and judge.
Hasidim and their critics have argued it out, and both sides would say they are guarding something precious.
Here, the rebbe is met as Hasidim meet him: a guide, and in Hasidic teaching, more than a guide.

how: Hasidim visit their rebbe for blessing and advice, gather at his tish on Sabbaths and festivals to hear his teaching and sing, and often write to him with requests for prayer.

o: the leader and guide of a Hasidic community
a judge who rules on disputes in a Jewish court
a scribe who writes Torah scrolls by hand

p: the Yiddish way of saying rabbi
a table, a gathering around the rebbe
the righteous one, a channel of blessing

s: every Jewish community follows a rebbe
the rebbe belongs to Hasidic life. some communities were wary of giving one person that much weight.
the Mishnah says make for yourself a teacher
Pirkei Avot: choosing a guide is something you do on purpose.
a rebbe only answers questions about prayer
followers bring him marriages, businesses, sick children, the whole of life.

games.q: you're at a rebbe's tish. he tastes a little of the food in front of him. what happens to the rest?
o: it's passed out into the crowd, and people reach for a crumb.
it's saved for the rebbe's family.
games.why: the leftovers go out to the followers. in Hasidic life, even a crumb from the rebbe's plate carries a blessing.

practice: Bring to mind one person who has helped you see your way: a teacher, a grandparent, a coach, a friend who told you the hard thing at the right time.
Picture their face, remember one thing they said or did that you still carry, and notice what let you trust them. If you pray, you can give thanks for them by name.

wordCard.voice: Rebbe. The Yiddish form of rabbi, and for Hasidim the leader of a community: a guide, and in Hasidic teaching, a channel of blessing. Today's word.

orig.note: Yiddish form of rabbi, used by Hasidim for the leader of their community.

carryVoice: Your line: a guide. The Mishnah's advice: make for yourself a teacher. Until tomorrow.
